title: Finding the Minimum in a Rotated Sorted Array

concept: Given a sorted array of unique integers that has been rotated between 1 and n times, find and return the minimum element. The original array was in ascending order before the rotation.

solutions.label: Linear Scan
solutions.summary: Scan every element and track the minimum value.

solutions.label: Binary Search
solutions.summary: Use binary search to identify which half contains the pivot and narrow down to the minimum.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Original Sorted: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7"] -->|"Rotate by 3"| B["Rotated: 4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3"]
    B --> C["Find Minimum"]
    C --> D["Answer: 1"]
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style D fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. Imagine you have a sorted array of unique integers in ascending order. Someone takes the last few elements and moves them to the front. This is called a rotation. Given such a rotated array, your task is to find the minimum element. For example, the sorted array one, two, three, four, five, six, seven might become four, five, six, seven, one, two, three after rotating by three positions.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So the array was originally sorted, then rotated some number of times. I want to confirm a few things. Are all elements unique? And can the array be empty?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great questions. Yes, all elements are unique. The array will always have at least one element, so you don't need to handle the empty case. The array length can be up to five thousand. Also, the rotation count is between one and n, where n is the array length.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. And I should return the minimum value itself, not its index, correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's correct. Just return the minimum value.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright. So to summarize, I have a rotated sorted array of unique integers with at least one element. I need to find and return the smallest value. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is a linear scan. I just iterate through the entire array and keep track of the smallest value I've seen. For the array four, five, six, seven, one, two, three, I'd compare each element and find that one is the minimum.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: It's O of n time since we visit every element, and O of one space since we only use a single variable to track the minimum.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. That gives us a baseline, but we're not using the fact that the array was originally sorted. Can you think of a way to take advantage of that property?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Definitely. Since the array has a sorted structure, binary search should help us narrow down the search space much faster.

sections.title: Binary Search
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    S["Array: 4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3"] --> Step1
    Step1["left=0 right=6 mid=3 val=7"] --> Check1{"7 > 3 right element?"}
    Check1 -->|"Yes: min is in right half"| Step2["left=4 right=6 mid=5 val=2"]
    Step2 --> Check2{"2 > 3 right element?"}
    Check2 -->|"No: min is in left half"| Step3["left=4 right=5 mid=4 val=1"]
    Step3 --> Check3{"1 > 2 right element?"}
    Check3 -->|"No: min is in left half"| Step4["left=4 right=4"]
    Step4 --> Result["Minimum = 1"]

    style Result fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style Step1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style Step2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style Step3 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: In a rotated sorted array, one half is always properly sorted and the other half contains the pivot. The key insight is: if the middle element is greater than the rightmost element, the minimum must be in the right half. Otherwise, it's in the left half including mid.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me walk through our example: four, five, six, seven, one, two, three. Left is zero, right is six, mid is three with value seven. Seven is greater than three, the right element, so the minimum is in the right half. We set left to mid plus one, which is four.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Now left is four, right is six, mid is five with value two. Two is not greater than three, so the minimum is in the left half. We set right to mid, which is five. Next, left is four, right is five, mid is four with value one. One is not greater than two, so right becomes four. Now left equals right, both at index four, so we return one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We halve the search space each iteration, so the time complexity is O of log n. Space is O of one since we only use a few pointer variables.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. That's the optimal solution for this problem.

O of n time
O of 1 space"] --> B["Binary Search

    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. We started with a linear scan at O of n time, then improved to O of log n using binary search by leveraging the sorted property of the array.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key takeaway is that whenever we see a sorted or partially sorted structure, binary search is worth considering. By comparing the middle element with the rightmost element, we can determine which half contains the minimum and eliminate the other half each step.
